questions.q: In a single round of the Prisoner's Dilemma, two purely rational, self-interested players cannot communicate or retaliate later. Mutual cooperation would leave both better off than mutual defection. What does classical game theory say two such rational players will actually do?
choices: Both will cooperate, since cooperation is the jointly optimal choice
Both will defect — defection dominates cooperation for each player individually, even though it leaves them both worse off
Each randomizes 50/50 between cooperating and defecting
They split — one cooperates while the other defects

questions.q: Premise 1: If it rains, the sidewalk gets wet. Premise 2: The sidewalk is wet. Many people conclude it must have rained. Is that conclusion logically valid?
choices: Yes, but only if it's currently cloudy
No conclusion can ever be drawn from an if-then statement
No — this is the fallacy of affirming the consequent; something else (a sprinkler, a hose) could have wet the sidewalk
Yes — the sidewalk being wet proves it rained

questions.q: Buses arrive at a certain stop following a Poisson process (perfectly memoryless and random) with an average of one bus every 10 minutes. If you walk up at a uniformly random moment, what is your expected waiting time for the next bus?
choices: It cannot be determined without knowing the exact schedule
5 minutes, half the average interval, since you arrive at a random point
10 minutes — memorylessness means your expected wait equals the full average interval, not half of it
